extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of modern Japanese literature; writers and translators studying Kawabata's style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and observable qualities for producing or evaluating prose in the manner of Yasunari Kawabata — spare, lyrical Japanese modernist fiction emphasizing suggestion, aesthetic simplicity, and themes of love, death, and isolation. Also includes Wikipedia-specific guidance for translating the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spare, lyrical, subtly-shaded prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Kawabata's prose is described as "spare, lyrical, subtly-shaded" and praised for "narrative mastery, which with great sensibility expresses the essence of the Japanese mind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor economy of language, lyricism, and subtle tonal shading rather than overt explanation; value delicate sensory detail and restrained emotional expression. Anti-pattern: florid, overtly expository prose that removes ambiguity or delicacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shinkankakuha — 'new impressions' / 'new sensations' in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Shinkankakuha movement (which Kawabata helped initiate) focused on offering "new impressions" or "new sensations"/"new perceptions" in literature, reacting against Naturalism and proletarian literature and influenced by Cubism, Expressionism, Dada, and modernist styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize perceptional freshness and novel ways of rendering experience; experiment with fragmented or nontraditional perspectives. Example: Bungei Jidai journal. Anti-pattern: merely updating older modes (e.g., calling it 'Neo-Impressionism') rather than generating new perceptual approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-for-art's-sake aesthetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Associated with an "art for art's sake" philosophy that resists didactic or overtly social/political agendas in favour of aesthetic experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow aesthetic concerns and formal experimentation to drive composition rather than moralizing or programmatic messaging. Anti-pattern: subordinating artistic form to external political or pedagogical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberately unfinished endings; emphasis on vignettes over conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Kawabata "left many of his stories apparently unfinished" intentionally — valuing vignettes of incidents along the way over conclusive endings — as part of his aesthetics to avoid sentimentalism or imposed morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open or fragmentary endings, let scenes speak for themselves, and avoid forcing closure. Scoring note: evaluate whether inconclusiveness serves the work (evoking ambiguity, resonance) rather than resulting from sloppiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Haiku-like form: brevity, suggestion, and what is left undrawn
rubrics_metrics.description: Kawabata equated his form of writing with the traditional poetry of Japan, the haiku — privileging brevity, suggestion, and what is implied rather than stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ compressed imagery, elliptical phrasing, and suggestive gaps; value negative space in prose. Anti-pattern: over-explaining or filling every gap with exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zen-influenced simplicity, space, and abbreviation
rubrics_metrics.description: In his Nobel Lecture Kawabata emphasized Zen Buddhism's focus on simplicity, isolation, and the importance of "space, abbreviation, what is left undrawn," using arts like ink painting, ikebana, and bonsai as analogues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for aesthetic restraint, careful selection of detail, and use of silence/absence as expressive devices. Example techniques: pared-down description, deliberate omissions that invite reader inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring themes: impossible love, impending death, melancholy
rubrics_metrics.description: Many works explore themes of "impossible love" and "impending death," melancholy, dawning eroticism offset with bitterness, and elegiac tones in postwar contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When emulating or evaluating, look for sustained thematic preoccupation with fragile human relationships, unfulfilled desire, and mortality rendered in understated ways. Anti-pattern: treating such themes with melodrama or sentimental resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of distance and character isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Kawabata often gives the impression that characters have built up a wall around them that moves them into isolation; his writing represents a pervasive "sense of distance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft characters whose inner separateness is shown indirectly through behavior, scene, and atmosphere rather than explicit statement. Evaluate how narrative distance contributes to mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of traditional Japanese cultural elements as structural/backdrop devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Kawabata uses cultural forms (e.g., the tea ceremony in Thousand Cranes, a geisha and hot-spring town in Snow Country, a Go match in The Master of Go) as settings and symbolic frameworks to explore inner feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate cultural rituals, games, or arts not merely as color but as structural or symbolic scaffolding that refracts characters' emotions and themes. Anti-pattern: using cultural detail superficially or exotically without thematic integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal and stylistic experimentation (stream-of-consciousness, scripts, varied modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kawabata experimented across styles: Asakusa kurenaidan echoes late Edo literature, Suishō gensō is "pure stream-of-consciousness," and he even worked on experimental film scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to vary narrative mode and to mix traditional and modernist techniques; assess whether experimentation enhances perceptual or emotional aims rather than functioning as gimmick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wikipedia translation/edit guidance (procedural standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article contains instructions: "Machine translation... is a useful starting point... translators must follow the LLM translation guideline, revise errors as necessary and confirm that the translation is accurate... You must provide copyright attribution in the edit summary..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating the article, do not copy-paste raw machine output; revise and verify with sources; provide interlanguage link and copyright attribution in edit summary; add the {{Translated|ja|川端康成}} template to the talk page if applicable. Anti-pattern: posting unverified machine translation without attribution.
